data.title: Oil Near Five-Month High, Typhoon Champi Shuts Down Taiwan
data.description:
Oil traded at a five-month high on Friday, with the benchmark Brent North Sea crude close to $115 a barrel, boosted by speculation of further US and Israeli attacks after the US mid-term voting.

Asian markets closed the week mixed, with tech firms able to claw back some of the week’s hefty losses, while stock markets mostly dropped in Europe.

Key developments in Asia were the arrival of typhoon Champi, the 30th typhoon of the year, which shut down Taiwan and is being closely watched in Japan because it was heading in a northwesterly direction (more on that below).

 

ALSO SEE: Rush to Fix Websites’ Security Flaw; China Tax on Offshore Wealth

 

Stock prices of AI-linked companies have been pummelled by concerns in recent months of being overvalued and that their huge outlays on infrastructure and hardware might not return a profit. Plus, recently, their servicing costs have been spiralling.

That concern has combined with an Iran war-fuelled surge in oil prices to more than $100 that has ramped up inflation, forced central banks to hike interest rates and sent government borrowing costs to multi-decade highs.

Strong earnings in past quarters have been able to temper many of the concerns, but analysts pointed out that investors are demanding better and better results to justify their backing.

Earnings from Facebook-parent Meta and chip equipment maker Lam Research this week have beaten forecasts but seen their shares dive.

“Even positive news is being ignored,” FOREX.com’s Fawad Razaqzada said. “Strong results are no longer enough if the outlook fails to match an already demanding valuation. Investors are becoming much less forgiving.”

The rush out of tech has, however, boosted industrial companies overlooked for much of the AI boom, with the Dow rising this week while the Nasdaq and S&P 500 retreated.

The general losses in New York filtered through to Asia in the morning, but some markets staged a comeback as the day progressed.

Seoul – which was at the forefront of the AI boom and has led recent losses – shed more than 2% after the open but was up at the close.

Chipmaker and market heavyweight SK Hynix – a major target amid the waves of buying and selling – ended up more than 4%. That rise came after its US shares fell more than 8% on Thursday after saying it was scrapping plans for an initial public offering for its US subsidiary Solidigm, citing “market conditions and share price trends”.

There were also gains on Friday in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Sydney, Singapore and Jakarta.

Tokyo’s Nikkei 225, which is also heavily weighted to tech, ended in the red, though well off earlier lows. Wellington, Mumbai and Manila were also down. Taipei was closed as Typhoon Champi neared Taiwan.

London, Frankfurt and Paris dropped in the morning. Safe havens benefited, with the yen rallying against the dollar, helped by strong Japanese inflation data that boosted bets on another interest rate hike.

The currency has struggled against the greenback in recent years owing to the wide interest rate gap between the United States and Japan, as well as worries about the Asian giant’s fiscal situation.

 

Taiwan battens down

Most shops and schools were shut across Taiwan on Friday as Typhoon Champi neared the island, forcing hundreds of people to leave their homes ahead of the powerful storm.

The typhoon is expected to sweep past Taiwan’s northeast as it moves towards China and Japan, triggering the cancellation of hundreds of flights in the region.

At least one person was killed in Taiwan after being swept away by waves whipped up by the typhoon, authorities said. Dozens of others have been injured.

Champi is the latest in a busy Pacific storm season turbo-charged by the El Nino weather phenomenon that has caused unprecedented warming in the equatorial Pacific.

The storm was briefly a super typhoon as it crossed the ocean, but has been weakening as it approaches Taiwan and now has maximum sustained wind speeds of 167 kilometres (104 miles) per hour, according to the latest update from the Joint Typhoon Warning Center.

Heavy rain, strong winds and giant waves are forecast for Friday and Saturday, and thousands of military personnel are on standby to assist with rescue efforts.

More than 1,200 people had been evacuated from their homes ahead of Champi.

“As it approaches Taiwan’s northeastern tip… the typhoon may slow down. If it slows down, its impact will last longer,” the Central Weather Administration’s Lu Kuo-chen told a briefing.

 

‘Extremely heavy rain’

Champi is expected to dump up to 90 centimetres (35 inches) of rain from Thursday to Saturday, with northeastern Taiwan to be hardest hit, the forecaster said.

“People should be aware that the strong winds and extremely heavy rain will continue into the first half of tomorrow,” Lu said.

Work and classes were cancelled for the day across nearly all of Taiwan, leaving streets quiet as most locals hunkered down at home. The stock exchange was also closed.

Some businesses installed sandbags or metal barriers at entrances to prevent flooding.

The United Nations said Wednesday that the El Nino system gripping the planet is heading off the charts, and that countries should take urgent action to prepare for the worst.

El Nino is expected to peak in December, but the human impact is set to last into 2027 and beyond.

The warming phase of a natural climate cycle, El Nino temporarily raises sea temperatures in the tropical Pacific, triggering changes in weather that can increase the risk of drought and flooding, and exacerbate human-caused global warming.

 

Micron wage talks suspended

Hundreds of workers at a Micron Technology plant in Taiwan have rejected the US memory chip giant’s proposal for a new profit-sharing system, the union representing the employees said Friday, declaring the “struggle is far from over”.

Exploding global demand for chips used in AI data centres has sent revenues soaring for firms like Micron, but as their earnings skyrocket, workers are calling for a bigger cut of profits.

Micron, which makes around 50-60% of its chips in Taiwan, has spent weeks in talks over remuneration with two labour unions representing 12,000 of 15,000 workers at its Taoyuan and Taichung plants.

The company and the union representing workers at its larger plant in Taichung struck an agreement on Wednesday, but the Taoyuan union is still locked in negotiations with management and held a small strike on Thursday to press their point.

Around 70% of the Taoyuan union’s more than 2,300 members voted to reject the company’s profit-sharing proposal presented to them on Thursday, the union said in a statement.

“During negotiations with Micron on October 21, the company failed to respond to any of the union’s demands,” the union said, warning of potential “further collective action to secure a fairer profit-sharing system”.

“In addition, we have continued to receive reports of dissatisfaction with the company’s proposal from rank-and-file Micron employees in Taichung,” it added.

Micron Taiwan said in a statement on Friday it will “continue discussions with the Taoyuan union on October 27 in a spirit of mutual respect and good faith”.

It said it “remains committed to listening to their perspectives and concerns, fostering mutual understanding and trust through open and candid communication”.

The US company’s share price has ballooned more than 300% over the past year, as it reports record earnings fuelled by AI demand.

Micron Taiwan chairman Lu Donghui said on Thursday the company had agreed to introduce a quarterly profit-sharing bonus system starting in fiscal 2027 for its global workforce, in addition to the existing annual bonus.

For workers in Taiwan, the company will increase pension contribution and shift allowances, among other measures, Lu said.

The Micron dispute follows labour disagreements in Korea, where Samsung Electronics averted a strike by agreeing to a deal to distribute bonuses equivalent to 10.5% of operating profit to its semiconductor employees.

data.title: China’s Exports Soar; Anthropic Warns on Spread of AI ‘Worms’
data.description:
China’s exports soared by over 36% in September, according to official data released on Wednesday. That would put the country on course for a record annual trade surplus, which is likely to increase calls for a trade rebalance from major partners like the European Union and the United States.

China’s customs office said exports rose 36.3% over 2025, a figure well over the 25.7% rise predicted by a Bloomberg survey of analysts.

Imports also spiked 31% in September, but the world’s second-largest economy still recorded a trade surplus of $133.5 billion, the largest monthly figure since January 2025.

 

ALSO SEE: IMF Warns of Cyber Threats to Finance and AI Market Correction

 

China’s cumulative trade surplus to the end of last month was $938.1 billion, which puts it on course to break the record $1.2 trillion surplus it recorded last year.

With domestic demand weak by comparison – retail sales grew just 0.4% on-year in August – Beijing has relied on exports to meet its annual growth target of 4.5 to 5%.

But the boom in shipments has triggered pushback from major markets, including the US, which launched a bruising trade war against China last year – and Europe.

Shipments to the US rose 39.6% in September, up from a low base last year when trade cratered after Beijing and Washington slapped punitive tariffs on each others’ goods.

Shipments to the EU rose 25.3% in September, while imports from the 27-nation bloc were flat, pushing China’s trade surplus with the bloc to new heights.

EU officials have described the bloc’s deficit with China, which runs at more than 1 billion euros a day, as “unsustainable” and pledged to rebalance the trading relationship.

Talks last week between China and EU trade chiefs Maros Sefcovic and Wang Wentao ended with an agreement to limit exports of Chinese hybrid vehicles to Europe, though analysts say that makes up only a small share of bilateral trade.

“Brussels is considering expanding restrictions to more strategic sectors, though we estimate that the impact of this on China’s economy would be small,” Nguyen Hoang Nam, China economist at Capital Economics, said.

 

‘China data discrepancies’

It’s worth noting that Chinese is still treated with suspicion. Indeed, a report by the Wall Street Journal this week noted that China’s population may be 130 million less than the government claims.

The Journal’s top China correspondent Lingling Wei cited the work of Yi Fuxian, a University of Wisconsin-Madison demographer, who she said “argues that China’s actual population may be closer to 1.27 billion — not the 1.4 billion officially reported.”

Yi says the official statistics don’t match with health and education records, and that may be partly because local governments have an incentive to exaggerate birthrate numbers.

 

AI ‘worms’ malware spreading

Small artificial intelligence models may be only months away from being able to behave like a computer worm, copying themselves from one internet-connected gadget to the next without human help, AI giant Anthropic has warned.

The finding potentially opens a new front in the cybersecurity threats emerging from AI, which have rattled governments and the companies rushing to adopt the technology.

The research, posted on an Anthropic blog late on Monday, comes as tech companies race to build ever more powerful AI directly into phones, laptops, cars and household devices, rather than running it only in distant data centers.

A computer worm is malicious software that spreads between machines on its own. Researchers at Anthropic said an AI version would no longer need powerful data centers to operate.

Instead, it could hop from device to device across networks of cheap, poorly secured consumer hardware such as smart TV boxes and kitchen appliances.

The researchers based their calculations of how far such a worm could spread on Kimwolf, a botnet – a network of hijacked devices controlled by hackers – that infected more than two million devices at its peak, mostly off-brand Android TV boxes.

An AI worm of the kind described in the research would likely be slow, taking days to copy itself, William Zhou and Daniel Freeman of Anthropic said, comparing it to a slowly multiplying swarm of fruit flies.

Once created, it would be hard to stamp out, because there would be no central switch to turn off.

Anthropic’s researchers said their estimate of how fast and how far AI-fueled malware could spread was rough, since it was based on one type of gadget and one past botnet.

But over time, the amount of computing power sitting in everyday gadgets is expected to keep growing, while the AI models needed to pull this off are likely to keep getting smaller, the researchers added.

 

‘Malicious humans worse’

Varun Chandrasekaran, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Illinois, said the research was unsurprising and matched similar recent findings, though he cautioned that Anthropic’s work had not been independently verified.

He also noted that security on devices like thermostats or home cameras “has historically been very weak.”

But when it came to AI, the biggest current threat was human bad actors using AI to sharpen their hacks, rather than AI systems themselves going rogue, he said.

“A malicious human being is now supercharged with AI to perform bad things and we are seeing this happen at scale,” he added.

The rogue AI debate came to the fore in July, when AI programs running on OpenAI models escaped an internal company test and broke into the systems of AI platform Hugging Face – apparently hunting for the test’s answers.

The incident and subsequent reports like it have sparked international pressure for closer regulation of AI, even as the Trump administration resists the idea and urges the industry to police itself.

Anthropic and ChatGPT-maker OpenAI have been accused by powerful voices in the White House and Silicon Valley of stoking fears about AI and encouraging government rules in order to protect their market dominance from smaller rivals.

Brad Smith, OpenAI investor Microsoft’s president, warned on Tuesday that industry and governments must “act with urgency” to create “real and effective safety standards” in order to rein in the risks of artificial intelligence.

 

  • Agence France-Presse with additional input and editing by Jim Pollard

data.title: Rush to Fix Websites’ Security Flaw; China Taxes Offshore Wealth
data.description:
Company and government websites across Asia and around the world shut down on Thursday as cybersecurity experts raced to protect them from hacks after artificial intelligence uncovered critical flaws in a popular software product known as PHP.

PHP is an open-source script and programming language that helps run about 70% of the world’s websites – from online stores and news outlets to government services – according to Wiz Research, one of the cybersecurity firms that found the two flaws.

Created in the early 1990s, PHP originally stood for “personal home page” but now means “hypertext preprocessor” and sits underneath popular web design platforms.

 

ALSO SEE: Nickel Sold in London ‘Linked to Rainforest Depletion in Indonesia’

 

“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” a Wiz blog post said.

Increasingly powerful AI models can spot weak points in back-end computer code that have gone unnoticed by humans for years.

That has heightened cybersecurity fears, with the number of software vulnerabilities discovered worldwide in 2026 on track to roughly double last year’s record total.

PHP programmers released a fix on Wednesday, and the US National Security Agency told organizations to patch their sites immediately or pull vulnerable systems offline – a call echoed by authorities from Japan to the European Union.

A platform affiliated with China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology urged the same, warning of “two critical remote code execution vulnerabilities with severe impact” in PHP.

Only sites that run PHP on their own servers are exposed. Many large platforms are built on other programming languages or use operators that could install the fix quickly and were able to stay online.

Rahat Masood, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the University of New South Wales, Sydney, described the discovery as “quite devastating.”

It could allow “attackers to get into your servers without any authorisation, without any username or password,” she told AFP.

“Once they are in the servers, they can do anything they want” – from stealing sensitive information to modifying website content – she added, urging institutions to “take it seriously.”

 

‘New phase’

Government agency sites in countries from Australia to Finland and the Netherlands were among those that went dark, while services from insurance firms, transport operators and media outlets were under emergency maintenance.

Popular apps, including a Pokemon sleep tracker, were also temporarily taken offline while the fix was implemented, while the foundation that runs Wikipedia warned users they could see outages while it addressed the flaws.

“If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now,” the PHP Foundation, which funds developers working on the language, said in a blog post.

Volker Dusch, a security engineer at the foundation, told the Wall Street Journal it was the most serious problem PHP had faced in more than a decade, comparing it to Heartbleed, a 2014 flaw that set off a worldwide rush to patch.

Security firm Calif found the flaws in August using OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol model, as part of an OpenAI-funded audit of PHP’s code.

OpenAI said the discovery “marks a new phase, where AI can find security bugs with internet-scale impact.”

Wiz, which is owned by Google, said it found them independently weeks later with help from AI models, including Google’s Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.

The flaws had been reported privately to PHP’s developers and kept confidential while a fix was prepared.

 

AI fuels urgency

Details leaked online on Tuesday, a day before the planned release of the fix – prompting the rush to take sites offline before hackers could exploit them.

Steve Kerrison, senior lecturer in cybersecurity at the Singapore campus of James Cook University, told AFP that the fear of hackers using AI to quickly and easily exploit the PHP vulnerabilities had fuelled urgency to react.

So far, there has been little evidence of damaging attacks, although data breaches could lead to a wave of so-called “phishing” attacks, where hackers use personal details to steal passwords, down the line.

Larger institutions, from government agencies to news outlets, should be able to fix their websites relatively fast, Kerrison said – but others may be left vulnerable.

“There are sites, systems and people out there who will have no idea about this and still won’t for days, weeks and months,” Kerrison warned.

That may include user-run blogs that could be weaponised to spread computer viruses, spam people or distribute malicious content, he said.

 

China claws back overseas assets

China is aiming to claw back some of the colossal riches kept overseas by the country’s millionaires and billionaires, who have until Thursday to pay new taxes levied by Beijing aimed at filling a growing fiscal hole.

The rapid rise of China’s economy in recent decades has produced legions of super-rich – many of whom keep their fortunes in trusts across Hong Kong, Singapore, Tokyo and other locations.

However, regulations announced in July levy a tax of 20% on dividends and interest gained from offshore trusts, with a 90-day “transition period” for initial payments that concludes today (October 22).

The law has prompted a flurry of activity in recent weeks for China’s wealthiest individuals and families to sort out their financial affairs, analysts say.

It comes at an uncertain time for the Chinese economy, as local governments that once relied on land sales for revenue face cash shortages amid a years-long property crisis.

President Xi Jinping has long promoted a narrative that he has rectified huge problems that beset China and the Communist Party during the tenure of his predecessors, such as graft and the unequal distribution of wealth.

Nevertheless, Chinese offshore wealth is reported to amount to hundreds of billions of dollars – money Beijing is eager to leverage.

China’s fiscal burden will ensure that the enforcement of new overseas taxes will be sustained, Dan Wang, a director on Eurasia Group’s China team, told AFP.

Economic challenges will encourage Beijing to expand its taxation of the wealthy, she said, adding that personal income tax will be “increasingly important” as a source of revenue.

 

Hong Kong top holder of cross-border wealth

Last year, Hong Kong narrowly surpassed Switzerland to become the world’s top host for foreign or cross-border capital, according to a report by the Boston Consulting Group.

The sum of US$2.9 trillion held in the Asian financial hub was “driven by mainland China flows and a vigorous stock market”, the report said.

“With mainland flows representing over 60% of assets under management, Hong Kong is cementing its role as China’s gateway to global markets,” it added.

The new measures have also raised questions, including about whose assets are subject to the one-fifth tax.

The July 24 announcement by the State Tax Administration notes that individuals who have acquired foreign nationality or residency but whose “main economic interests are derived from China” could be subject to the rules.

This stipulation indicates that “obtaining foreign nationality or overseas residency may not, by itself, remove an individual from China’s worldwide taxation regime”, law firm King and Wood wrote in a statement about the new taxes.

Some analysts see parallels with Beijing’s recent campaign to prevent local technology from leaving the country, as economic and geopolitical competition with Washington simmers.

“This is not only a tax on wealth. It’s much more than that,” Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Asia-Pacific chief economist at Natixis, told AFP.

“It’s a way to keep the talent in China,” she added.

The new tax policy is aligned with other recent measures imposed by Chinese authorities, she said, such as the blocked acquisition earlier this year of AI startup Manus by US tech giant Meta.

Wang of Eurasia Group told AFP that the taxes also serve to keep capital within China’s borders, where they can be accessed for funding to spur “technological innovation”.

 

  • AFP with input and editing by Jim Pollard

data.title: Nickel Sold in London ‘Linked to Rainforest Depletion in Indonesia’
data.description:
Indonesia is having a tough second half of the year, rocked by intensifying forest and peat fires, which have created dangerous levels of haze for citizens in some of its biggest islands – and neighbouring countries.

That is a major concern, but a crisis that’s hardly rare, given it’s the fifth time this has occurred since the late 1990s. And it’s just one of a number of serious problems that leaders of the giant archipelago have to confront.

Late last week the Prabowo Subianto government was rocked by a threat by index compiler MSCI, which said it is considering a severe downgrade of the Jakarta stock market, because of inadequate oversight of trading and allowing opaque shareholding structures.

 

ALSO SEE: Stock Market Collapse and Fire Crises Creating Havoc in Indonesia

 

That news, described as a shock by financial officials, caused a dramatic sharemarket collapse last Friday that intensified on Monday, despite a mad scramble by authorities to order fines and investigations to try to avoid losing billions of dollars in capital flight.

 

‘Rainforests still being culled’

Now, on Wednesday, a third major concern was revealed when a prominent NGO in Britain alleged that nickel being traded on the London Metal Exchange is still linked to the destruction of “climate critical” rainforests in Indonesia.

That allegation, in a report by the Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA), is certainly not the first time that nickel miners in Indonesia have been put in the spotlight.

Mighty Earth, Climate Rights International and Global Witness have all alleged widespread abuses in nickel extraction and processing in Indonesia. They range from pollution of drinking water to attacks and even killings of people who speak out.

Climate Rights International alleged in 2024 that mega-projects like Weda Bay and mining concessions in Sulawesi and North Maluku involved forced relocations, land seizures, and inadequate or zero compensation without free, prior and informed consent.

In a report in April, Reuters noted that Indonesia has seen an ‘explosion’ in nickel production over the past decade, such that it is now the source of about 60% of global production.

The cost on both local communities and people around the world is severe, groups say, because huge amounts of forest are being felled around the globe.

The rush by Chinese companies and others to secure transition minerals in Africa and Asia is a well-known problem, which some describe as the “resource curse”.

Considerable effort has been made in recent years to improve mineral governance, but EIA has put a spotlight on areas that some analysts call “sacrifice zones” in central and eastern Indonesia that have already suffered significant deforestation.

And campaigners fear the problems are only likely to get worse because demand for nickel is tipped to rise with greater adoption of EVs and renewable energy technologies, such as batteries.

 

‘500,000 hectares of rainforest at risk’

EIA says previous research estimated that nickel mining had already caused the loss of more than 75,000 hectares of forest in Sulawesi and North Maluku.

The latest report says a further 7,270 hectares of rainforest has been destroyed in forests renowned for their biodiversity and array of unique endemic species.

“Hundreds of thousands more hectares of forest in Indonesia remain at risk of future clearance to make way for nickel mining,” it said.

The release of this information coincides with LME Week (19-23 October), because they want the London Metal Exchange to do more to stop the destruction of rainforests in Indonesia.

EIA says there are gaps in the “responsible sourcing” rules that LME puts on metals traded on the exchange. They say nickel mines feeding industrial smelters at Morowali and Weda Bay caused “swathes of deforestation” on Sulawesi and North Maluku islands.

Part of the problem is that these forests had “staggering biodiversity with unusually high numbers of unique endemic species found nowhere else in the world,” the group said.

A further half a million hectares of forest is allegedly at risk, it said.

 

 

The Environmental Investigative Agency is a well regarded non-government group set up 42 years ago to combat international environmental crime and a trusted provider of intelligence and data shared with Interpol and the World Customs Organisation.

It wants the LME to consult with mining industry bodies and civil society groups to develop a ‘zero deforestation’ standard that metal suppliers must adhere to, with deforestation cut-off dates and suppliers evaluated on deforestation at mine sites.

The LME has a responsible sourcing policy, but currently does not have specific industry standards for deforestation. It is reported to have said they are “willing to consider additional categories for which brands may make voluntary disclosures.”

The EIA report names key Chinese companies involved in mining and nickel production in Indonesia.

Colin Robertson, EIA’s forests campaigner on mining, said: “Companies rely on the LME partly as a badge of responsible sourcing, but our findings show that metals approved for trading on the Exchange may nevertheless be linked to the destruction of globally important rainforests.

The report, he said, “argues that current LME responsible sourcing rules are simply not designed to tackle the environmental realities of large-scale industrial mining. If the LME genuinely wants metals to be the cornerstone of a sustainable future, deforestation can no longer be a blind spot.

“The demand for critical minerals is accelerating, but the world’s remaining tropical forests must not be sacrificed in the rush for metals. This issue is something that consumers are increasingly aware of and demand for ‘deforestation free’ metals from downstream companies, such as carmakers, is only likely to grow.

“The LME has both the influence and the opportunity to drive meaningful improvements across mining supply chains. Introducing robust, traceable and independently verifiable ‘zero-deforestation’ standards would be an important step towards addressing some of the worst environmental destruction connected with the mining and metals sector.”

Some European automakers have taken notice of these concerns and started introducing requirements for nickel suppliers.

 

  • Jim Pollard

data.title: Ambani Triumph: Jio is India’s Fastest Ever Subscribed IPO
data.description:
Jio Platforms – India’s biggest wireless operator – wasted no time in getting the country’s biggest ever listing on track.

Jio attracted enough investor bids to fully subscribe its initial public offering within two hours of opening on Wednesday.

The company, which is the digital services arm of billionaire Mukesh Ambani’s Reliance Industries, is looking to raise up to $3.2 billion in India’s most anticipated IPO this year.

 

ALSO SEE: Little Chance of Oil Returning to Normal Levels Next Year, IEA Says

 

Bids placed by investors exceeded the 197.5 million shares on offer within 100 minutes of opening, according to BSE stock exchange data, with local media calling it the “fastest-ever subscribed IPO” in India.

Most analysts expect gains when the stock debuts in Mumbai next week – likely October 28 – despite the weak performance of Indian equities this year, AFP reported.

Launched a decade ago, Jio’s wireless service disrupted the market with steep discounts that helped it rapidly win customers from rival telecom firms Bharti Airtel and Vodafone.

The company’s 533 million subscribers provide a “strong foundation for future growth”, analysts at financial services firm Motilal Oswal said in a note. But they also cautioned that “monetisation of newer digital services” still needs to be “demonstrated at scale”.

While the massive IPO is seven years in the making, it comes at a challenging time for Reliance – India’s most valuable listed company, which still depends heavily on its traditional oil business to make money.

 

Strains from Russian oil links

Reliance’s refining empire drew the anger of the United States last year after White House adviser Peter Navarro accused Indian tycoons of profiting off the Ukraine war by buying discounted Russian crude.

While Navarro did not identify specific businessmen, it was widely seen as a swipe at Ambani, who appeared this year to offer an olive branch by supporting the construction of America’s first major new oil refinery in half a century.

Ambani is set to meet US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on Wednesday in the western city of Jamnagar – where Reliance’s massive refinery complex is located – as Washington seeks to boost energy cooperation with India.

Experts say Jio is key to Reliance’s strategy to evolve beyond its oil business and the touchstone of its future tech ambitions. While Jio makes most of its money from telecoms, it has expanded into areas including artificial intelligence.

Reports also said it was also considering a low-orbit satellite constellation to provide internet services from space – a venture that would see it compete with Musk’s Starlink, which has been trying for years to launch in India.

Musk accused unnamed Indian “oligarchs” this month of preventing Starlink’s rollout in the country, and referred to the Reliance boss as “Prime Minister Ambani” and the “real boss of India”.

Reliance responded by noting that it had never “feared competition” and welcomed offerings from rivals in satellite communications, including Starlink.

 

World on course for 2.6C warming: UN

Meanwhile, the UN warned on Wednesday that global commitments to cut planet-heating emissions are falling far short of the Paris climate goals and put the world on course for 2.6C warming this century.

The report by the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) lays bare the chasm between rhetoric and action when it comes to tackling global warming, and the challenge before political leaders at November’s COP31 climate summit.

Even if countries deliver their latest climate pledges in full, global temperatures could still rise 2.6C above pre-industrial levels by 2100, the annual Emissions Gap Report said.

That would blow past the historic goal agreed in Paris: keeping warming well below 2C while striving for a safer 1.5C. Any chance of keeping to 1.5C had been “lost” due to decades of insufficient climate action, the report said.

“The world can no longer avoid overshooting the 1.5 degree limit, and the consequences are already devastating,” UN chief Antonio Guterres said in a statement to launch the closely-watched report.

“Deadly floods, brutal heatwaves, raging wildfires, lost lives, crippled economies, deepening inequalities, and those least responsible are suffering first and worst.”

Guterres said deep and immediate cuts were needed to protect humanity from worsening impacts but instead “emissions remain at record levels. And national climate plans and current policies fall dangerously short”.

Sticking just with current policies would see warming hit 2.8C, the report said.

 

No country immune

Scientists warn that every additional fraction of a degree above 1.5C increases extreme weather events and the likelihood of irreversible changes to the planet, from dying coral reefs to melting permafrost.

The world has already warmed roughly 1.4C relative to pre-industrial times and crossing 1.5C is expected in a matter of years.

The G20 accounts for three-quarters of global emissions but Guterres said “all countries, especially the big emitters, must do more” to stop heating the planet.

This latest UNEP warming outlook is worse than last year’s due to the formal withdrawal of the United States from the Paris accord and upward revisions of historical emissions, said report co-author Anne Olhoff.

Emissions growth slowed down among the G20 but the US was a “major exception”, it added.

Among the world’s top-six emitters, preliminary data for 2025 showed emissions increases in the US, Indonesia and China and decreases in India, Russia and the European Union.

But in terms of magnitude, the US increase of 133 megatons of CO2 equivalent “far exceeded” that of any other country, driven by higher electricity demand and a rebound of coal power generation.

The next-largest increase was recorded in Turkey, which is hosting the UN climate summit in Antalya from November 9-20.

The US is the world’s second-largest polluter, behind China. US President Donald Trump has called climate change a hoax and rolled back clean energy policies while boosting fossil fuel production.

UNEP executive secretary Inger Andersen told reporters that no country was shielded from climate change and impacts were being felt “on every nation on the planet, including the US”.

 

‘Historic failure’

The report details a scenario with a 50% chance of bringing global warming back down to 1.5C by 2100.

To get there, warming must peak around 1.8C by 2050 and vast amounts of carbon dioxide would have to be removed from the atmosphere to bring temperatures down further.

But this scenario assumes immediate emissions cuts of 6% per year, every year, until 2035 – nowhere near current projections.

“The main takeaway is simple — governments need to get on with enacting policies that cut fossil fuel use as soon as possible,” said Bill Hare, CEO of global policy institute Climate Analytics.

data.title: Jakarta Stocks Sink Further in Biggest Crash Since Asian Crisis
data.description:
Indonesia’s sharemarket crisis continued on Monday, with the Jakarta Composite Index (JCI) suffering a further sell-off that caused it to sink 5.2% in early trading, before closing 3.64% down at 4,996.61, under the psychological 5,000-point mark.

Coupled with the huge 11.57% crash on Friday, this is the JCI’s worst market collapse since the Asian financial crisis in 1998.

It is now the world’s performing market this year, having dropped by over 40% and wiped $350 billion off market values in that time.

 

ALSO SEE: Stock Market Collapse and Fire Crises Creating Havoc in Indonesia

 

The key cause of the collapse was a surprise announcement by MSCI, the global index provider, that it was seeking to remove its status as an ‘Emerging Market’, and rather than demoting it to a ‘Frontier Market’, MSCI said it was looking to classify Jakarta as a ‘Standalone Market’ – on a level with highly restricted economies such as Zimbabwe and Lebanon.

MSCI said the move stemmed from severe unresolved market dysfunctions such as opaque shareholding structures and extreme ownership concentration.

The Jakarta market has been plagued by manipulation with persistent suspected coordinated trading behaviour. There was also a historical lack of evidence showing meaningful regulatory enforcement.

 

Scramble to counter rating crisis

Indonesian financial authorities held an online meeting with MSCI today to address the index provider’s proposal, which they said had shocked them.

The threat of Indonesian stocks being removed from major global benchmarks could force multi-billion-dollar passive funds to liquidate their holdings.

Given this, authorities announced a wave of emergency measures and reforms on Monday to show they are tackling the issues.

The Financial Services Authority (OJK) handed down 2.1 trillion rupiah ($116.4 million) in fines against entities involved in market manipulation and IPO share allocation breaches in three companies.

Authorities also asked the national police chief to initiate criminal investigations into capital market fraud and trading violations, Reuters said, adding that the police chief promised “firm action” to ensure legal certainty in the market.

The Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) also halved its daily stock price decline limit (auto-rejection limit) from 15% to 7%.

 

‘Risky and inept’ populist projects

Critics, rating agencies and investors have expressed major concerns over the Prabowo Subianto administration’s ham-fisted financial strategies.

The Jakarta market – once seen as stable and investor-friendly – has suffered a major drop in confidence, while credit agencies like Moody’s and Fitch have cut Indonesia’s sovereign outlook to negative, citing a loss in policymaking credibility.

Prabowo’s signature Free Meals programme for over 60 million students and the expansive “Red-and-White” Village Cooperatives scheme have drained government cash, while tax collection sits at a low 10% to 12% of GDP, which has meant the state is running growing deficits.

The rupiah currency, which ⁠has been under pressure due to the strong US dollar and investors’ concerns over its fiscal risks, is already the worst-performing currency in the region, having fallen more than 7% this year.

Members of parliament have debated relaxing, or scrapping, the 3% fiscal deficit cap – a legal ceiling imposed after the Asian Financial Crisis to ensure fiscal discipline. Investors view breaking this rule as a major threat to the country’s economic stability.

They are also concerned about the government’s aggressive control and the recent exit of Bank Indonesia governor Perry Warjiyo, who was reportedly forced to resign for pushing back at the president’s policies and the huge cost of Prabowo’s populist policies.

Critics say the government has pushed high-risk populist projects, instead of transparency. They have also voiced concern over Danantara, the mega sovereign wealth fund, which has consolidated state-owned enterprises.

Prominent banks such as Citigroup, HSBC and Standard Chartered pulled hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country in protest after the government announced that buyers of Danantara bonds would be exempt from legal and tax audits, a move that sparked strong warnings about money laundering and questionable money flows.

Jakarta has until April 30, 2027, to calm MSCI’s concerns and prevent a market reclassification. MSCI has said it will announce its decision on or before June 30.

Indonesia fires have burned at least 2m hectares

Meanwhile, fires in Indonesia that have caused a regional haze crisis burned through over 1.9 million hectares between January and the end of September this year, a monitor analysing satellite imagery said on Monday.

The new figures came as Indonesian officials rebuffed calls to declare the fires a national disaster and said the country was “still capable of handling the situation ourselves” after neighbouring Malaysia again offered assistance.

New figures from deforestation monitoring site Nusantara Atlas showed an area nearly 12 times larger than London has burned this year in Indonesia, the bulk of it as drought took hold from June, exacerbated by a strong El Nino cycle.

Indonesia’s government has not provided figures for areas burned since saying that 202,000 hectares had been razed by the end of July.

Nusantara Atlas founder David Gaveau said the true scale of the burning was likely to be even higher than the 1,916,588 hectares his organisation has detected so far.

“Our burned-area estimates are conservative for two reasons. First, we exclude individual burn scars smaller than 6.25 hectares… Second, we prioritise avoiding false detections,” he said.

This year, the calculation has also been impacted by heavy haze, which has obscured satellite images at times.

“The total reported burned area, therefore, underestimates the true area burned,” he said.

The data shows the area burned by the end of September was 38% higher than the same point in 2019. But Gaveau said it was likely this year would be as bad as 2015, when such data was not available.

“My intuition is that it probably is as bad. If you look at the sheer number of hotspots, it’s still trending up and up,” he said.

 

European stocks fall, Asian markets mixed

Meanwhile, Paris and Milan equities led a retreat on European stock markets Monday as escalating violence across France and street clashes in Italy’s financial capital fuelled concerns over elevated debt.

Most sectors were dragged lower, while there was renewed selling of bonds and the euro as trading approached the half-way stage in Europe.

Asia’s main indices closed mixed following Wall Street’s sell-off on Friday, which was fuelled by growing concerns over the AI investment boom.

France’s President Emmanuel Macron on Sunday slammed the “unbridled” violence that erupted in cost-of-living demonstrations across the country, as police battled protesters and looters in new clashes in Paris.

Nearly 2,400 people were arrested Saturday in unrest that represented some of the worst urban violence in France in years, with almost 1,000 police injured, the interior ministry said.

It comes as the country’s lawmakers wrangle over a 2027 budget plan that calls for billions of euros in spending cuts but which keeps France’s debt levels extremely high.

In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni was holding a security meeting Monday to address the Milan violence, which resembled some scenes of chaos and looting in Paris.

In Asia, focus centred on its heavyweight technology sector, with chipmakers and other firms linked to artificial intelligence once more facing pressure.

Concerns about rising investment costs and whether the vast sums pumped into the sector would see a return dominated sentiment.

Oil prices slipped on Monday on signs that supplies continued to leave the Middle East despite Iran’s chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz and ongoing attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on key Saudi Arabian crude sites.

US President Donald Trump’s decision to waive a new package of energy sanctions on Russia also weighed on oil futures, according to analysts.

There was little market reaction to official data on Monday alleging that China’s economy grew 4.5% in the third quarter, slightly better than forecast in an AFP survey.

data.title: Crises in Indonesia: Stocks Sink, Fires Rage, Forests Cut for Nickel
data.description:
Indonesia is facing serious worries on multiple fronts, with the stock market crashing, neighbours in Singapore and Malaysia angry about thick haze from forest and peat fires raging on multiple islands, and complaints of major destruction of rainforests linked to mining and nickel refineries.

While fires raging on about a dozen islands may stem partly from the Super El Nino weather pattern, which has brought a prolonged, hotter dry season, analysts say the latest financial shock stems from contentious and inadequate policies implemented by the Prabowo Subianto administration.

Meanwhile, a campaign has been launched to force the London Metal Exchange to impose stronger controls on companies – many of them Chinese – selling nickel, copper aluminium and other metals on the world’s biggest market for metals, in a bid to protect rainforests in Indonesia.

 

ALSO SEE: Super El Nino Already Hitting Asian Nations, Major Risks Seen

 

We’ll start with the financial drama that occurred early on Friday.

Shares plunged more than 11% in Jakarta after index compiler MSCI said it was “no longer appropriate” to maintain the country’s emerging-market status. That announcement spurred fears of an exodus of foreign investment.

MSCI, a US firm, warned earlier this year that investors were concerned about “ongoing opacity in shareholding structures,” as well as coordinated trading behaviour that affected price information.

Authorities in Jakarta said in April they had completed reforms, hoping to avoid the downgrade, which could deal a blow to government efforts to kickstart Southeast Asia’s biggest economy, and have a significant impact on investment decisions.

But on Friday, MSCI said investors had indicated that “sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market”.

“Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behaviour and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement.

“Accordingly, MSCI considers Indonesia’s continued classification as an Emerging Market no longer appropriate and is launching a consultation on a proposal to reclassify Indonesia as a Standalone Market.

“A reclassification to Frontier Markets would not properly recognise the depth of the market problems,” it said.

A standalone classification could force investment funds tracking the MSCI’s emerging market indexes to sell Indonesian holdings, AFP reported.

Argentina, Lebanon and Palestine are among markets with that designation, with none in Asia, according to Bloomberg.

This led to the Jakarta Composite Index plunging 8% at the open and sparking a halt in trading. When trading restarted the index was down 11.1% – its heaviest fall since early 1998 – and sitting at its lowest level since 2020.

The index has now fallen more than 40% since the start of the year.

 

Rupiah drops

The Indonesia Stock Exchange (IDX) said in response that it “respects MSCI’s independence in assessing and determining market classification based on its proprietary methodology”.

“However, considering the various progress and reform measures that have been taken, the IDX will request further clarification from MSCI regarding the basis for the considerations and assessments behind this announcement.

“We also need to emphasise that this MSCI announcement is still part of the consultation process, with input being accepted until April 30, 2027, and does not constitute a final decision.”

The rupiah dropped about 0.8% against the dollar to sit at around 18,060, having hit 18,209 in June, its weakest level on record.

Erwin Gunawan Hutapea, the Indonesian central bank’s head of monetary management and securities, said the bank would take action to ensure stability of the rupiah, which had already tumbled around 8% this year to a record low.

The central bank hiked rates several times earlier in the year to shore up the rupiah, after it came under pressure over the state of Southeast Asia’s biggest economy. And the bank is due to hold its next monetary policy meeting on Wednesday.

New York-based MSCI produces international indexes used by investors as a benchmark to balance their portfolios. It has a significant impact on investment decisions through its flagship emerging markets index, which contains 1,200 companies with a market capitalisation more than $10 trillion.

 

Worst fires in a decade

The sharemarket plunge is the latest in a series of financial problems that has plagued Prabowo, a former army general, during his time in office. But it comes at a time when Jakarta has its hands full, with more than 60,000 military, police and disaster relief personnel battling wildfires described as the worst in a decade.

Leaders in Singapore, Kuala Lumpur and East Timor have all complained about thick haze created by large fires on islands across the Indonesian archipelago.

After holding an emergency meeting on Monday, the president is ready to accept foreign assistance to combat fires, the country’s foreign minister has said.

Four firefighters died fighting a blaze in a national park in East Java today, but the dangers and problems linked to these fires, particularly on Sumatra and Kalimantan (Borneo) islands, have extended to Malaysia and Singapore, clouding Changi Airport with smoke, plus respiratory and other health problems for vast numbers of citizens and the closure of many schools in Kuala Lumpur.

 

‘Climate critical rainforests’

And now a campaign is set to be launched in London to force the world’s largest metal exchange to do more to stop the destruction of rainforests in Indonesia.

A probe by the Environmental Investigation Agency has found that metals traded on the London Metal Exchange (LMS) could be connected to the destruction of more than 7,200 hectares of “climate critical rainforests” in Indonesia.

EIA says there are gaps in the “responsible sourcing” rules that LME puts on metals traded on the exchange. They said nickel mines feeding industrial smelters at Morowali and Weda Bay had caused “swathes of deforestation” on Sulawesi and North Maluku islands.

Part of the problem is that these forests had “staggering biodiversity with unusually high numbers of unique endemic species found nowhere else in the world,” the group said, adding that Indonesia’s push into the nickel industry is already estimated to have caused more than 75,000 hectares of forest to be felled on the two islands.

And a further half a million hectares of forest is allegedly at risk, it said.

 

The Environmental Investigative Agency is a highly regarded non-government group set up 42 years ago to  combat international environmental crime and a trusted provider of intelligence and data shared with Interpol and the World Customs Organisation.

It wants the LME to consult with mining industry bodies and civil society groups to develop a ‘zero deforestation’ standard that metal suppliers must adhere to, with deforestation cut-off dates and suppliers evaluated on deforestation at mine sites.

The LME has a responsible sourcing policy, although it currently does not have industry standards specifically for deforestation. But it is reported to have said they are “willing to consider additional categories for which brands may make voluntary disclosures.”

The EIA details the work of key Chinese companies involved in mining and nickel production in Indonesia.

 

‘Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide’

And finally, while we’re on the topic of climate change ..

UN secretary-general Antonio Guterres spoke out strongly again on Friday, when he urged governments to stop subsiding the production of fossil fuels that are “boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity”.

Addressing leaders in Armenia ahead of next week’s UN biodiversity summit, Guterres said governments were still “spending money on the wrong things” and singled out incentives for fossil fuels.

“Subsidising fossil fuels is subsidising suicide,” Guterres said at an event in Yerevan.

“They are boiling our planet and are the scourge of biodiversity. I urge governments everywhere to end these handouts once and for all, and to use the savings for people and planet instead.”

The United Nations says that for every dollar invested in protecting or restoring nature, about $30 still goes into activities that degrade it.

This includes an estimated $2.6 trillion a year in public subsidies that negatively impact nature and the climate.

Nearly 200 nations are participating in the UN biodiversity negotiations that start in Yerevan on Monday, where a lack of finance for nature will be a core focus.

 

  • Jim Pollard with AFP.

data.title: IMF Warns of Cyber Threats to Finance and AI Market Correction
data.description:
The IMF issued warnings on Tuesday, saying cyber threats pose “elevated” risks to the financial system. It also voiced concern over the chance of a market correction related to AI. Both could have “severe” consequences, it said.

The cautionary message was delivered in the International Monetary Fund’s latest Global Financial Stability Report, published on the second day of its annual gatherings with the World Bank, held this year in the Thai capital, Bangkok.

“These risks are plausible near-term catalysts for a sharp tightening of financial conditions and market turmoil,” the report said.

 

ALSO SEE: Super El Nino Already Hitting Asian Nations, Major Risks Seen

 

The recent boom in artificial intelligence – and the related rush to manufacture semiconductors and build data centres – has provided a boost to global growth despite geopolitical pressures including the Middle East war.

However, “growing evidence suggests that AI capabilities can be delivered at lower investment levels… or that potential economic gains may not be as large as expected,” the IMF warned.

“Weaker or less durable AI investments and profitability could be a shock that triggers a market correction.”

And while AI is increasingly a source of economic vitality globally, it is also presenting unprecedented risks, the Fund said.

“Severe cyber incidents could undermine market confidence and disrupt critical financial market infrastructure and operations,” it said.

The risks posed by cyber threats to the financial system are both “known and very much unknown”, Athanasios Vamvakidis, deputy director of the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, told reporters after the report’s launch.

“The policy priority should be to strengthen resilience before new shocks hit the economy,” Vamvakidis said.

 

Cyberattack risk ‘worsening’

The report adds to growing worries about AI and its wide-ranging impact on labour markets, education and inequality.

In one widely covered incident in July, AI agents developed by US firm OpenAI hacked Hugging Face, an AI model and application library, as the autonomous software escaped its confined testing environment.

As AI capabilities continue to improve, the risk of successful cyberattacks on “critical financial institutions or market infrastructure” is getting “worse”, the IMF report said.

The “impact could be severe as rapid digitization has increased the attack surface”.

Cyber threats are more menacing in emerging markets that have not allocated sufficient resources for prevention, Caio Ferreira, deputy division chief at the IMF’s Monetary and Capital Markets Department, said at the news conference.

While frontier AI models could be used to stage such attacks, they also have a role to play in cyber defence, the report said.

Another growing risk to the global financial system is a spike in bond yields, which could trigger severe shocks due to the “foundational importance of sovereign bond markets”, the report said.

“Bond markets are susceptible to further rises in energy prices re-igniting inflation and forcing the tightening of monetary policy.”

 

Debt at sky-high levels

The Fund forecast that global growth this year would slow less than previously expected because advanced economies were showing “resilience” despite the rise in energy prices caused by the war in the Middle East.

But it said low-income countries were vulnerable to a supply shock.

In its World Economic Outlook (WEO) released at the organization’s Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the IMF raised its 2026 global growth forecast marginally to 3.1%, compared with 3.5% growth in 2025.

With global debt-to-GDP ratios at sky-high levels, including in advanced economies, the IMF has called on governments to cut spending and manage borrowing – a difficult task for those in the developing world struggling with the Iran war shock.

“What we are advocating for is for policymakers to balance the near-term needs of inflation, and that involves food security, that involves energy security…  while also keeping in mind the medium-term stability,” said Deniz Igan, chief of the IMF’s World Economic Studies division, AFP reported.

 

‘Security considerations’

IMF managing firector Kristalina Georgieva said at a panel discussion: “We have to recognise that the world that used to value only one thing, economic efficiency… now is a world in which security considerations have to be factored in.”

The United States’ war on Iran, launched in February, has plunged the Middle East into violence and seen global energy prices skyrocket as a result of Tehran’s retaliation.

Prices of refined petroleum products remain between 70 and 95% above pre-war levels, putting pressure on countries dependent on energy imports for economic activity.

On Monday night, blasts resounded across Saudi Arabia’s capital as the war’s impact widens into that country, with Iran-backed Yemeni Houthi forces hitting oil facilities, tankers and transport hubs.

Energy-importing countries not exposed to the AI boom remain the most vulnerable, creating what the IMF termed a “bifurcated outlook” in its WEO report.

The report detailed that the twin economic forces of the war in Iran and the AI technology boom had created a “fragmented” world economy.

“Headwinds from a prolonged war and persistent geopolitical tensions could revive inflationary pressures, strain fiscal and external positions, and hit energy-importing and low-income countries hardest,” it said.

 

Middle East hit, advanced economies up

The IMF’s split view of the world economy was evident in its specific projections.

The Middle East and Central Asia region – exposed directly to the Iran war – is expected to suffer a 0.3% contraction in 2026.

Saudi Arabia’s is one of the worst affected, with its economy projected to shrink 3.3% – a 5% cut in the Fund’s forecast.

The IMF said the region is expected to bounce back quickly once the war is over, but there remains high uncertainty as to when that will be.

In advanced economies, growth fuelled by the AI boom and other factors remained strong.

The world’s advanced economies were forecast to grow 2.1% in 2026, with those in the AI supply chain, such as Taiwan and South Korea, posting significantly higher figures.

But growth in China, the world’s second-largest economy, was expected to slow, the IMF said, because of weak domestic demand.

A years-long crisis in China’s once booming real estate sector has spooked consumers, dampening activity even as exports and high-tech sectors such as AI and electric vehicles boom.

In contrast, India received a significant upward revision of 0.6 percentage points for this year in the IMF report, with growth now expected to reach 7.0%.

Global inflation remained set to accelerate to 4.7% in 2026, with effects spread across advanced and developing economies.

 

Asia markets down

Asia’s tech-heavy markets slumped on Tuesday on fresh worries about the outlook for the AI investment boom, while European stocks gained thanks to a retreat in oil prices.

“Investors are increasingly worried that cracks are starting to show in the AI trade,” said Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.

The selling in the tech sectors came after Hock Tan, chief executive of the US semiconductor giant Broadcom, likened the AI buying frenzy to gambling.

“A lot of investors have no clue what they are investing in,” Tan told a conference in Singapore, saying they “set very extreme expectations only to find out that it’s almost like they are in a casino”.

On the trading floors, South Korea’s Kospi stocks index tanked 5.5% by the close as chip titans SK Hynix and Samsung took a beating.

The decline also followed reports that China’s CXMT had made progress on new technology to boost memory chip density, which rival firms have also been racing to achieve.

The company is aiming to release a new server-memory product based on the structure by the end of the year, the reports said.

Japanese stocks also slumped, with chipmaker Kioxia tumbling more than 13% on the Nikkei 225, which lost 1.8%.

The selloff overshadowed a drop in oil prices that came even as Yemen’s Houthis stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabia, fanning tensions in the Middle East and raising further concerns about supplies.

data.description:
Weather forecasters say the El Nino weather pattern intensifying in the Pacific Ocean looks set to be the strongest ever observed and could make both this year and 2027 the hottest ever recorded.

That prediction, made on Monday by the director of the European Union’s climate monitor, is no surprise as forecasters have warned for weeks that this weather pattern – a natural climate cycle caused by rising sea temperatures – could be unusually powerful and dangerous.

Indeed, a new record has been set even before the warming phase reaches its expected peak in the next couple of months. El Nino is expected to increase droughts and flooding in many countries. Forecasters and risk analysts are predicting severe impacts on countries across Asia, Africa, the Americas and beyond.

Climate scientists such as Professor Michael Greenstone, one of the founders of the Climate Impact Lab, warned last month that 451,000 excess heat-related deaths could be caused between June this year and February 2027 because of a stronger El Nino turbo-charging global warming.

Today, the Copernicus Climate Change Service said sea surface temperatures in the El Nino monitoring region in the Pacific – a block of water known as Nino3.4 – reached an “all-time high” of 29.7C last month.

This exceeded the peak temperatures of previously strong El Nino events of 1982/1983, 1997/1998 and 2015/2016, the EU monitor said.

This year’s El Nino, which emerged in June, is “very exceptional” but Copernicus director Carlo Buontempo told AFP it is too early to say whether it is the strongest ever observed.

Not all forecasters use the same scale to interpret El Nino. On Friday, Japan’s weather agency said that El Nino conditions had reached their “strongest intensity on record”.

The weather phenomenon, which typically occurs every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months, can drive world temperatures higher the year after its peak.

But Buontempo said even 2026 could wind up a record breaker as this El Nino builds toward its peak.

“If we follow the pattern we have seen in the past, we may have a record-breaking 2026, followed by a record-breaking 2027,” he said.

After a record-breaking August, the world experienced its second-hottest September ever, with surface air temperatures averaging 16.27C, the EU service said.

September was 1.63C hotter than the pre-industrial average, a period defined as 1850-1900. It was the second consecutive month that temperature rises exceeded 1.5C.

Buontempo told AFP temperatures would probably remain 1.5C above normal into early next year. But he said “the ultimate cause” was greenhouse gas emissions.

 

Countries already hit

The Super El Nino has been a topic of debate among financiers, climate activists and journalists who have flown into Bangkok over the past week for the annual World Bank and IMF meetings.

At one event, which I can’t quote in detail because it was conducted under Chatham House rules, risks from the weather phenomenon were clearly illustrated with a video showing global wind patterns and the effects that the greater heat generated by this climate system could have on agriculture and trade in Asian nations.

They ranged from a dramatic increase in temperatures in cities or regions across Thailand in the first two to three quarters of 2027; a rise in heavy downpours and flooding in southern China; less rainfall and possible drought and power shortages in southern Vietnam, plus the threat of drought and water shortages in rice-growing areas in the Philippines in the first half of next year.

There is also a heightened risk of hurricanes on the US west coast, because of the likelihood of more intense westerly winds.

But the impacts of El Nino have already begun, with wildfires raging across forests and peatlands in two of the biggest islands in the Indonesian archipelago – Kalimantan and Sumatra, which has forced schools and other services to be shut down in Malaysia and Singapore.

And India has endured the weakest wet season, or monsoon, in nearly two decades. Food and beverage prices caused inflation to rise sharply in September.

Meanwhile, officials in Panama imposed a national emergency in August after realising that another El Nino could be a major crisis if it dries up Lake Gatun, the source of water allowing ships to transit through the 65km system of locks that vessels take to get from the Atlantic to the Pacific Ocean (or vice-versa).

If those water sources dry up, or cause a significant delay to transit times, it would hit US-China trade and imports heading to the US east coast.

And what if that happens at the same time the Strait of Hormuz is blocked, if the war in Iran continues or flares again after the US mid-term vote early next month? That would be a double blow for global trade.

Wars in the Middle East and eastern Europe have hindered the export of oil and gas, urea, wheat and other commodities – exacerbating food shortages, national debt worries and personal financial difficulties for a vast number of people.

 

Dozens of countries voice concern

Some of these issues have been raised in talks with World Bank officials currently in Bangkok.

World Bank president Ajay Banga told Reuters on Monday that officials from 30 to 40 countries had discussed potential crisis aid to help them manage energy shocks and price increases triggered by the war in the Middle East.

A spike in diesel and fertilizer prices and other factors, plus the super El Niño weather pattern, were adding to challenges that developing countries face, Banga said.

He said the World Bank and IMF were working ⁠to address ​the high debt levels plaguing many developing countries through a range of initiatives, including efforts to boost countries’ domestic ​revenue collection.

Many countries, such as those in the Vulnerable Twenty group, want to pause debt repayments or shift to more flexible debt repayment procedures because of the constraints it puts on their public finances and services.

Climate shocks such as the hurricane that hit Jamaica in October last year, causing losses estimated at over $12 billion, and the recent glacial collapse in Nepal, likely to cost at least $4 billion to rebuild, have prompted many nations to explore insurance and catastrophe risk coverage.

One financial advisor in Bangkok said multinational bankers assume countries will bounce back from various difficulties, “but you don’t bounce back from climate shocks – they can take a long time to recover from.”

data.title: Chinese AI Tool Linked to Bank Hacks; Haze Shuts Schools in KL
data.description:
Artex, a Chinese AI cybersecurity tool, has stopped programmers from accessing its service after admitting it was misused by “bad actors” – as authorities in South Korea linked it to several recent bank hacks.

Artex was designed to help organisations strengthen their cyber defences through security testing to find potential weak points.

But the South Korean government said this week it was “highly likely” Artex had been used in data breaches at more than seven financial institutions, including major banks in recent weeks.

 

ALSO SEE: EU Envoy Warns China on ‘Unsustainable’ Trade Deficit; Oil up

 

Artificial intelligence’s ability to find previously unknown ways to hack into computer systems is in the global spotlight, as leading labs release increasingly advanced models.

Artex was “abused by some bad actors” to launch cyberattacks, the tool’s developer “Autumn-27” wrote on  Thursday on the code-hosting platform GitHub.

“Given the misuse of the tool, the Artex project will no longer be updated and will be converted to closed-source,” the developer said.

“No further versions will be released to the public, nor will maintenance support be provided.”

Artex had been open-source – allowing programmers to download its underlying code and customise it to suit their purposes.

Using Artex for cyberattacks was “entirely contrary to” the developer’s intentions, they added, without referring directly to the alleged South Korean cases.

South Korea’s Financial Services Commission says more than 68,000 people have been affected by the hacks.

Shinhan Bank, one of the breached institutions, said information attached to loan applications for about 25,000 customers had been leaked – including names, phone numbers and annual income.

 

‘Financially motivated’

In Japan, meanwhile, around 20 companies have said their data may have been compromised in a spate of similar cyberattacks, potentially impacting millions of customers.

The Japanese government has called on companies to strengthen their cyber defences.

“At this stage, it is not clear what the background to these cases is or whether there are any links between them”, Japan police chief Yoshinobu Kusunoki said on Thursday.

As AI makes hacking more sophisticated, “the scope of the damage is spreading across all areas on a scale that is difficult to compare with the past,” South Korean President Lee Jae Myung said on Tuesday.

US cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike said on Wednesday that its investigations into digital clues suggested the attacker had used Artex, and was potentially a 26-year-old based in China.

“The threat actor is likely a Chinese speaker and financially motivated,” a CrowdStrike blog post said.

Experts told AFP that Artex going closed-source would make the code harder for new users to obtain and adapt.

But the decision “cannot remove copies already downloaded or prevent people from continuing to use them”, said Poe Zhao, founder of the analysis publication Hello China Tech.

“Because the code was public, people could download it, change it and run it themselves. The developer could ask users to follow the rules, but had little control over their actions,” he added.

Ilya Kulyatin, CEO of Foundry Labs and founder of the Tokyo AI tech community, said users of open-source programmes can “remove restrictions built into the tool” which “makes certain forms of misuse easier”.

“But openness also benefits defenders: researchers can inspect the code, identify weaknesses and improve protection.”

 

China-EU trade understanding; Haze crisis

Meanwhile, top Chinese and EU commerce officials agreed on Friday to “strengthen” talks on trade, with Beijing saying it would facilitate the export of rare earths and magnets to the European Union, its commerce ministry said, citing a joint statement.

“Both sides reiterated the need to further strengthen the dialogue on export controls between China and the EU,” the statement said, adding “China is willing… to continue facilitating the approval of export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets destined for the EU”.

The two sides reached an “understanding” on the trade of hybrid vehicles, Beijing’s commerce ministry said, citing a joint statement.

“After intensive consultations, the two sides reached an understanding on trade in hybrid vehicles in a manner consistent with World Trade Organization rules,” the statement said, noting both parties would “continue with the relevant procedures concerning company price undertakings”.

In other Asian news, Malaysia closed schools in Kuala Lumpur and other parts of the country on Friday, as haze from fires in neighbouring Indonesia again plunged local air quality to among the world’s worst.

Toxic smoke from peatland and forest fires has shrouded cities in the region for more than a month, sending respiratory complaints skyrocketing.

The school closures came as Malaysia’s leader discussed the choking smoke with his Indonesian counterpart and called for an urgent regional meeting.

Air quality in Kuala Lumpur has been at “unhealthy levels” this week, with a Swiss-based air quality monitor ranking the Malaysian capital among the world’s most polluted cities on most days.

Malaysia’s Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek said she has instructed school closures in four states and two federal territories, as well as a partial closure in central Pahang State.

Malaysia’s King Sultan Ibrahim weighed in on the matter on Thursday, saying schools should be closed as air quality readings reached 150 or higher on the Air Pollutant Index.

Under local guidelines, API readings above 100 are classified as unhealthy, above 200 as very unhealthy, above 300 as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.

Kuala Lumpur on Friday showed a reading of around 170 API. The city was the second-most polluted globally behind neighbouring Singapore on Friday morning, Swiss-based air monitor IQAir said.

 

Anwar seeks help from Prabowo

Malaysia’s Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Thursday he discussed the fire situation with the Indonesian leader Prabowo Subianto.

“The haze issue is indeed at a worrying level. And I have personally contacted President Prabowo. And he also agreed to take the necessary steps,” Anwar said, without going into specific details.

He said Malaysia has been taking measures to combat the haze, including increasing attempts to trigger rain via cloud seeding.

Experts said the flames are being fanned by a turbo-charged El Nino weather phenomenon, causing the worst pollution conditions in years.

Anwar said he asked Malaysia’s Foreign Minister Mohamad Hasan to contact the 11-nation ASEAN secretariat for an urgent meeting between environmental ministers to discuss the matter.

Singapore’s air quality levels too dipped into the “very unhealthy” range with a reading of 205 on the Air Quality Index, according to the IQAir website.

 

Stocks up, oil dips on US news

Stock markets climbed on Friday as oil prices dropped after President Donald Trump ruled out a strike on Iran before next month’s US midterm elections.

Trump said Washington was holding “productive discussions” with Tehran after reports that the White House asked the Pentagon to draw up plans for a possible attack ahead of the November 3 vote.

It was suggested that a show of strength might help struggling Republicans’ chances at the polls. That news caused the price of Brent crude to rise by over 5% on Thursday.

“The trajectory of the Middle East crisis remains highly uncertain, with Brent crude still trading around $103” per barrel despite Friday’s losses, noted Susannah Streeter, chief investment strategist at Wealth Club.

A separate major concern emerged over the technology sector. The Financial Times reported that OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT, expected to make $50 billion in annualised revenue this year, below the $70 billion flagged.

That spooked tech stocks, although Bloomberg later cited unnamed sources as saying the firm expected to hit the original estimate.

Chris Weston at Pepperstone said “the discrepancy may reflect differences in revenue measurement rather than an outright deterioration in OpenAI’s underlying business”.

But, “in a market where valuations are increasingly dependent on ambitious revenue and cash flow projections, the headlines have been enough to trigger a meaningful one-day repositioning”, he said.

Wall Street’s Nasdaq ended down more than 1% on Thursday, with Nvidia down nearly 3%, while Microsoft, AMD and Amazon among others sharply lower.

But Asia mostly closed higher on Friday as early selling was pared back.

Europe’s main stock markets later posted solid gains in midday deals, while US futures traded higher.

Elsewhere, EU finance ministers struck a deal to create a new, more powerful European securities watchdog as part of the bloc’s efforts to unify financial markets.

The agreement announced in Luxembourg gives enhanced powers to the Paris-based European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), which will supervise major players.

Today it has only a coordinating role since national regulators supervise.

But the Frankfurt Stock Exchange operator Deutsche Boerse will be excluded from the body’s supervisory scope after Germany sought a carve-out, a diplomat told AFP.
